title: Next Door to a Dead Pin

blocks.text: Overnight, someone put a new red pin on the dead-pin board, beside Greyfell.
I count them every morning, so I saw it before the tea urn was hot. Thirteen this year. The third within two hinges of Greyfell.
Cressida took the card down herself, read both sides, and put it in her coat.
"Full kit," she said. "Ninefold. Tomorrow."
"Is it contagious?" I said.
"Is there evidence it's contagious?"
Footnote: there was not. That was what bothered me.

The card said Ashcombe, distance 20, one hinge past Greyfell. Its doors had stopped opening six days before; the board runs about a week behind, because red pins wait on the Far Map clerk and the Far Map clerk waits on nobody. Cause, in the clerk's round hand: natural decay.
"I'd like to measure it," I said. "The decay."
Cressida was writing the crew list. She did not look up. "With what?"
I had a list. I always have a list.

1. Doors. How many reach the dead branch, and when each one stopped. 2. People. Anything odd they report, dated and timed. 3. Records. What Greyfell's Survey wrote about Ashcombe before it went. 4. Me. Whether anything happens to me.
"Strike four," said Cressida.
I struck four.

It was day thirty-two. My name had been settleable for two days. Footnote: on day thirty I wrote to Weirside's Exchange Desk asking for a meeting at the door where the swap was charged. No reply yet. I check the desk twice a day. I have decided this is normal.

Cressida's licence reaches distance 32, so she led. Brisk piloted. Standing Order 6.3: a trainee may accompany any crew within the leader's licence. Greyfell is distance 19. The furthest I had ever been was 2. Footnote: seventeen hinges further from home than I had ever stood, and I had packed a tape measure.
The stay was planned at three days. Seven is when rent starts. Three is a comfortable number.
Gideon had the kit room open by the time I came down with my bill.

"Greyfell, chuck?" He took my pen out of my hand before I could write with it. "Not with that. Steel nibs never caught on out there. Nor friction matches." He opened a drawer marked GREYFELL AND FAR and gave me a goose quill, already cut. "The pin card lists what they haven't got. Read it, or the door reads it for you."

Glare beats ballast. Footnote: a steel nib that can't exist at distance 19 is the first thing the doorway would take on the way out, and my counterpart would wake holding a pen nobody in his world could make. I wrote my bill in pinned ink with a quill and left the nib in the drawer.
Gideon hummed while he checked the quill's point against the light. Then he weighed my ink bottle in his palm, the way he does, and handed it back without comment, which from Gideon is a compliment.
Brisk came in and turned out every pocket onto the counter without being asked. A box of matches. She put it in the drawer next to my nib.
"Good, chuck," said Gideon.
"I'm older than you," said Brisk.
"How old?"
"Twenty-six."
Footnote: that is a new one.
Form 9, line one: My given name is Edric. Line two: I can take shorthand at ninety words a minute. Line three: My father is Tobin Ardent. Line four onwards, smaller.

My ballast I had made the night before, at home on Weir Lane, with the door shut and my mother asleep down the landing. Kind: coined word. I made a word, said it once into a pillow so that it was learnt by an act and not just thought, and have not said it since. Then I scratched a mark on a pebble as a spare, an hour later, so the word would be the older and would go first. In my kinds ledger, under a new heading, Greyfell, I wrote the kinds and not the designs. Footnote: the design of a ballast is the one thing I never write down. Paper is a witness with a long memory.

Day thirty-three. The Ninefold's south wall, the iron-studded door. Brisk stood in it with Greyfell's route on a card in her left hand and didn't look at the card once. Nineteen hinges. She read them like a grocery order, and the door opened on the first reading. The Bole side's opening for the day.
"Nine," said Brisk. "Vesey."
Cressida stepped through.
"Eight. Ardent. Move."
I moved.

Greyfell's Tessary is built of slate. In the Bole the quarry on the north fell was never opened; here, two centuries ago, someone opened it, and the whole city went grey to the gutters. The Ninefold Hall is the same stone as ours, because it is older than every one of Greyfell's hinges, but the threshold room has brass plates on every door, polished, with the name of each branch it reaches.
"Seven," said Brisk, behind me, and stepped through on six.
Greyfell's threshold warden met us at the plates: Surveyor First Wenna Dace, about fifty, in fingerless mittens, with a logbook under her arm like a second ribcage.
"You'll be here about Ashcombe," she said.
"We're here about decay," said Cressida.
Dace looked at her for a moment. "Same thing, I suppose. Come and see the Brackwater doors. They're the busy ones."

Brackwater is Greyfell's other neighbour, also distance 20. It split from Greyfell over a reservoir. Greyfell's Water Board built theirs on the fell; Brackwater's chairman, a man named Absalom Reay, cast the deciding vote for the estuary marsh, and the city there has made its tea with slightly salty water ever since. Greyfell's surveyors cross to it daily.
"Daily," I said. "Your kinds."
"Rota," said Dace. "Thirty surveyors. Nobody crosses more than once a fortnight. It's how a hall makes thirty-one kinds last."
Footnote: I liked her at once.

Four doors in Greyfell's threshold room reach Brackwater. I logged them: plate, width between jambs, height to lintel, mason's mark, which hand the latch was on. Door one, the old west door, was in use. Greyfell's desk clerk, Mr Pocock, a narrow man with ink on both cuffs, had read Greyfell's side of the route to hand the day's packet through. Through the open door I could see Brackwater's threshold room: the same stone, no brass plates, a woman at their desk in a brown shawl reaching out across the threshold for the packet.
Brisk counted under her breath. She can't help it. Any open door, anyone's opening.
"Three. Four."
I had my tape on door two.
"Five."
Door one went out.

There was no sound. The Brackwater clerk's hand was there, and then the doorway was only a doorway, and through it was Greyfell's map store, a mop in a bucket, a shelf of rolled charts. The packet dropped onto Greyfell's flagstones. Pocock was still holding the string.
In the same breath, two people were on the floor in front of door four.

They were in Greyfell field coats, on their knees, as if someone had set them down hard. One was a young man with a sunburnt neck. The other was a woman of about forty with grey in her plait. Both of them had their hands flat on the stone.
"Kell," said Dace. "Ruddock." She was already kneeling. "You went in by four, six days ago. You weren't due back till four."
"We were in the hall," said Kell. "Their hall. We were in the hall and then we weren't."

Dace stood up and sounded door two: Brackwater's route, plus the hinge of one of Brackwater's own pinned branches on the end. A sounding warms a door if the branch at the end is there, and spends nothing. Footnote: she couldn't simply read the route; Pocock had spent Greyfell's opening to Brackwater for the day. Nothing warmed. She sounded door three. Nothing. Door four. Nothing. Door one, the one I had just watched, she sounded last, with her palm flat on the frame.
Nothing.
I looked at my watch, because a surveyor should, and wrote the time down: 14:06, day thirty-three. Every Brackwater door cold in the same breath.
"That isn't decay," I said.
Cressida said nothing.
"Decay is a word for something slow," I said. "That was one breath. That was a fall."
Footnote: I said it too loudly. Dace's logbook was open, and she wrote it down.

Kell's bill was clean. Thrown visitors pay the normal exit, and his ballast had paid it; he had made it the morning they went in, and it had had ten hours left to run. Ruddock read hers twice. Her ballast had settled at midnight. She had made it the day before she went in, six days ago, and the seventh midnight after making it fell on her last night in Brackwater. She had planned to come home at four, with nothing in her pocket but her bill.
The line that now read false said: The summer I was eight, at my uncle's farm at Thrale.
"I remember a summer," said Ruddock carefully. "On a boat. In salt water." She looked at the cold door. "I think that's hers."

Footnote: somewhere on the far side of that door, Brackwater's Ruddock now remembers a farm, and the farm is in a world that has started to come apart. It cost her nothing she chose. It cost her anyway.
I made a list, because I was frightened.

1. The Bole is not on Brackwater's side. Brackwater is one hinge further out than Greyfell. Whatever fell, fell outward. 2. Our door home is a Greyfell door, and Greyfell is standing. 3. My ballast is in my head, unsaid. My spare is in my pocket, unseen. 4. I would like to go home now.

Cressida sounded the iron-studded door: the route to the Bole, with the weir night on the end, which is the route to Weirside. It warmed under her hand. If Weirside was there, so was the Bole. She didn't read the Bole's route itself; that would have opened the door and spent Greyfell's opening for nothing.
Footnote: the first time the weir night has ever been good news.
"Stated plan was three days," she said.
"I wanted to measure decay," I said. "This isn't decay."
"Then measure what it is."
I struck four.
They came in the morning.

Greyfell's Survey keeps a stray-fact desk; Dace said it had been taking a report or two a day for the past week, since Ashcombe. "A trickle," she said. By eight on day thirty-four there was a queue down the Hall steps and into the slate street.

I took a table. Dace gave me Greyfell's Brackwater files: a copy of Brackwater's ward roll, a box of desk letters, and a Brackwater glossary her surveyors had kept for twenty years, for the words that differ.

A baker named Mrs Hobb woke knowing a word. "Skell," she said, and looked embarrassed. "The white crust in a kettle. I've never had a crust in a kettle. Our water comes off the fell." The glossary had it: skell, Brackwater, kettle scale from estuary water. The ward roll had a Hobb, baker, on the same street in Brackwater.

A drayman with a fresh white scar along the back of his left hand. No injury; his wife had looked at the hand every night for thirty years and would have noticed. Brackwater's ward roll had him, drayman, same yard.
A boy of eleven who knew the tide tables. Greyfell's river is not tidal past the weir. Brackwater's ward roll had him.

An old man, a widower who had never married, who sat down at my table, folded his hands, and told me he remembered his wife's laugh. He described it carefully. I wrote it down. Brackwater's ward roll had him at the same address, with a wife.
Footnote: I wrote it down in ordinary ink. It was the only thing anyone could do for her.

By noon I had thirty-one reports. I checked every name against Brackwater's ward roll. Thirty-one had a Brackwater self. Nobody who lacked one had received anything. I drew it as a table, Greyfell names down the left, Brackwater facts across the top, and every row had a match.
Cressida read the table standing up. She read it twice.
"Windfall," she said.
That was all she said. She did not say what windfall implies, which is that something has to be falling. I noticed her not saying it. Footnote: I am noting it now.
Brisk brought me tea at two. "Kettle's got skell in it," she said. "Joke. Their water's lovely." Then, more quietly: "You've got the look. The list look."
"I'm fine."
"You're on item four."
I was. I struck it again.

Then I did item three. Dace let me have Greyfell's threshold log for Ashcombe, the dead pin I had come to measure. Greyfell had three doors to it. Eight days ago, at the dawn opening, the first went cold in the middle of a reading. Dace's surveyors sounded the other two within the quarter-hour. Cold. Nobody had been inside, so nobody was thrown home. But it was all in one morning, and it was all the doors.
"Your clerk called it natural decay," I said.
"Our clerk called it that too," said Dace. "It's the word on the form."
Footnote: if you measure decay twice and get the same answer, which is one breath, you have not measured decay.
Simeon Bray came in at dusk. He was the Hall's archive clerk, a tidy man with a grey face, and he did not join the queue. He went straight to Dace, and Dace brought him to me.
"His Brackwater self was a surveyor," she said. "Bray of Brackwater. Second. I've handed him letters through that door for nine years."
Bray sat down. "I woke up with a page in my head," he said. "Not a feeling. A page. Somebody showed it to him once, across a desk, under a lamp. He stared at it a long time. I can see every line."
"Can you draw it?"
He could. He asked for a ruler. He drew for two hours while the windfall queue thinned outside and Greyfell lit its lamps with tinderboxes. I watched him over his shoulder.

It was a route chart from Weirside. Thirty-nine hinges, the first of them the weir night, laid out the long way, in Weirside Survey notation: hinges numbered from the far end, hinge-makers' initials in little boxes. I knew the notation because I had spent a day in Weirside's registry on day zero, reading their cards until my eyes ran. Bray had never seen a Weirside card in his life. He reproduced the boxes exactly. He reproduced the letterforms.
Dace took the last six hinges to Greyfell's pin book and came back.
"Calder Fold," she said. "Distance 38 from your Bole. Dead pin since spring. Filed as decay."
Footnote: two hinges short of the cut line.
"There's a note in the margin," said Bray. He put the pencil down; his hand was shaking. "I'll do it tonight. I want to get it right."
"Get it right," said Cressida.
Day thirty-five, dawn. Dace brought the drawing to the iron-studded door in an envelope. Greyfell paper. Footnote: Greyfell paper is possible in the Bole. It stays.
"Read it at home," said Cressida. "We have an opening."
Brisk stood in the doorway and read the route home from Greyfell's side. Greyfell's opening for the day. The door opened on the first reading.
"Nine. Vesey."
Cressida stepped through. The doorway took its fee. On the Bole side she unfolded her bill under the lamp, Standing Order 9.1, read it, and said, "Clean."
"Eight. Ardent."

I stepped through with the envelope inside my coat. A small tug. Nothing I could name. The word went. I knew it had gone because I tried to find it, and where it had been there was only a sense of having once had a word. Bill out. Read. Every line true.
"Clean," I said.

Footnote: my counterpart in Greyfell now knows a word that nobody else in any branch knows. He lost nothing for it. He has a word for nothing, which is a better bargain than most of Greyfell got this week.
"Seven," said Brisk, and came through last, as pilots do. Bill. Read. "Clean."
Kinds logged for Greyfell: one each. In my ledger, under Greyfell: coined word, spent day thirty-five. The pebble in my pocket will settle at its seventh midnight and stop being anything at all.
Brisk counted the rest of it down to one anyway, out of habit, with all three of us already home.
That evening I took the envelope to my desk in the trainees' room, under the window, and laid the drawing out flat.
Thirty-nine hinges. Calder Fold at the end of them, dead since spring. Boxes of initials I couldn't read.
In the right-hand margin, beside the last hinge, Bray had drawn the note, small and slanted, the way it must have been written. A dagger, and then:
Cold by morning. Not decay.
I looked at it for a long time. Then I took out my own Form 9 and laid it beside the drawing.
The same slope. The same flattened g. The same dagger, with the little hook at the foot, the one I have drawn for footnotes since I was seven because a dagger looked more serious than a star.
I didn't write it.
He did: my counterpart, who has my hand and my name, has stood two hinges short of the cut line and footnoted it.
